name: Cloudera, Inc. (including Hortonworks)
subcategory: Hadoop / big-data platform; hybrid data cloud
key_takeaway: Cloudera and Hortonworks are the Hadoop era's natural experiment in degrees of openness. Both IPO'd, neither thrived alone, they merged, the combined firm closed distribution rather than the licence, and private equity took it private in 2021. The Apache projects outlived both companies' independence.

name: Cockroach Labs, Inc.
subcategory: distributed SQL database (CockroachDB)
key_takeaway: Cockroach Labs shows that a database company can move from Apache to nearly proprietary with little community backlash when the project lacks a large independent contributor base or a hyperscaler with motive to fork. The cost is that it now competes as a proprietary vendor against Apache-licensed rivals (YugabyteDB, TiDB) and Postgres itself, with no public exit and a valuation last set at the 2021 peak.

name: Confluent, Inc. (an IBM company since 2026)
subcategory: data streaming platform (Apache Kafka)
key_takeaway: Confluent shows a middle path: keep the engine at a neutral foundation, monetize a cloud service and proprietary or source-available extras. It avoided the Elastic/Redis-style fork, grew to $1.17B in revenue, and was bought by IBM for ~$11B in March 2026. Together with HashiCorp, it shows IBM consolidating open-source-origin infrastructure companies, after Red Hat, as a strategy for enterprise AI.

name: Couchbase, Inc.
subcategory: NoSQL document database
key_takeaway: Couchbase is the private-equity version of the consolidation that IBM drove with HashiCorp and Confluent: a smaller open-core database that moved to BSL in 2021, stayed flat in public markets, and was taken private by Haveli Investments for about $1.5B in September 2025, at roughly its IPO price.

name: Docker, Inc. (formerly dotCloud)
subcategory: containers / developer tooling
key_takeaway: Docker is the case of an open project that won its market so completely that the company struggled to capture the value: Kubernetes and the clouds monetized containers, Docker sold its enterprise unit in 2019, and then rebuilt around paid Desktop subscriptions for large companies. Value capture came from a proprietary client, not from relicensing the engine.

name: Elastic N.V. (formerly Elasticsearch BV)
subcategory: search and analytics engine (Elasticsearch, Kibana)
forks: OpenSearch (and OpenSearch Dashboards), forked from Elasticsearch/Kibana 7.10.2, first released April 2021
key_takeaway: Elastic is the canonical relicense-fork-reversal story. Closing the licence protected Elastic Cloud from AWS resale, but it handed AWS the moral high ground and a permanent, foundation-governed fork that splits the ecosystem. Three years later Elastic re-added an OSI licence (AGPL), keeping SSPL/ELv2 alongside. The company stayed public and growing throughout, so the closing was not fatal, but it permanently lost sole control of the search-engine standard it created.

name: Grafana Labs (formerly Raintank)
subcategory: observability (Grafana, Loki, Mimir, Tempo, Pyroscope, k6)
key_takeaway: Grafana Labs is the main counter-example in this group: it chose an OSI copyleft licence over a source-available one, avoided any fork, and kept compounding its private valuation (over $6B in 2024). Elastic (2024) and Redis (2025) later re-added AGPL themselves, which makes Grafana's 2021 choice look like where the relicensing wave settled.

name: HashiCorp, Inc. (an IBM company since 2025)
subcategory: infrastructure automation (Terraform, Vault, Consul, Nomad, Packer, Vagrant)
forks: OpenTofu (Terraform fork from 1.5.7, accepted by the Linux Foundation 2023-09-20; CNCF Sandbox 2025-04-23) and OpenBao (Vault fork, started 2023-11-09 under LF Edge)
key_takeaway: HashiCorp is the case where relicensing came late in the company's life and preceded a sale. The BSL change likely made HashiCorp a cleaner asset for an acquirer, and IBM bought it within about 18 months, even though IBM engineers had led the open Vault fork. The open-source community kept its own copy of Terraform (OpenTofu, now in CNCF), so the open standard survives outside the vendor.

name: InfluxData, Inc. (formerly Errplane)
subcategory: time-series database (InfluxDB, Telegraf)
key_takeaway: InfluxData is 'closing by feature' rather than by licence: the code stays MIT/Apache, but the features enterprises need are paid. It avoided forks, but its modest funding and undisclosed valuation point to a smaller outcome than peers that relicensed or went public.

name: Kong Inc. (formerly Mashape)
subcategory: API gateway / API management
key_takeaway: Kong is the 'stable open core' control case: Apache-2.0 gateway, paid enterprise features and SaaS, no licence change found, and private valuations rising from $1.4B (2021) to $2B (2023). It contrasts with the database companies that relicensed their cores.

name: Lightbend, Inc. (formerly Typesafe; d/b/a Akka)
subcategory: JVM reactive frameworks (Akka; formerly Scala and Play tooling)
key_takeaway: Akka is the small-scale version of the HashiCorp story: a 2022 BSL switch quickly produced an ASF-governed fork (Apache Pekko, top-level by May 2024) that key downstream projects adopted. Even a mid-sized ecosystem now forks into a foundation when its licence closes.

name: MariaDB (MariaDB plc / MariaDB Corporation and the MariaDB Foundation)
subcategory: relational database (MySQL fork)
key_takeaway: MariaDB exists because MySQL changed hands: it is a founder-led fork to keep the code under community control, backed by a nonprofit foundation. Its company struggled (SPAC listing, then a roughly $37M private-equity take-private) while the GPL server persists, separating the robustness of the code from that of the company. It also wrote the Business Source License used across the later relicensing wave.

name: MongoDB, Inc. (formerly 10gen)
subcategory: database (document / NoSQL)
key_takeaway: MongoDB is the clearest case of an open-source-origin company that closed its license and still kept growing: SSPL protected its managed-service business from cloud resale, and the market rewarded it with roughly a 20x rise from its IPO valuation. But closing the license did not remove competition, it moved it to the API layer, where the hyperscalers now back an MIT-licensed, foundation-governed alternative. For an openness study, MongoDB shows that a strong first-party cloud product, not the license, is what captures value, while openness mainly bought the early adoption.

name: MySQL AB and Sun Microsystems (MySQL's path to Oracle)
subcategory: relational database (MySQL)
key_takeaway: MySQL is the founding case for this group: a dual-licensed open-source company that sold for about $1B in 2008, then passed to Oracle with Sun in 2010. Ownership change, not relicensing, drove the community fork (MariaDB), whose company later wrote the BSL used in the relicensing wave.

name: Neo4j, Inc. (formerly Neo Technology)
subcategory: graph database
forks: PureThink's redistribution of Neo4j Enterprise with the Commons Clause removed
key_takeaway: Neo4j fought a fork of its relicensed code in court rather than in the market, and won, the opposite of OpenSearch or Valkey, where hyperscaler backers made forks durable. Closing Enterprise did not dent growth: about $550M raised, a $2.2B valuation and over $200M in revenue by 2024, with IPO preparation reported.

name: Redis Inc. (formerly Garantia Data, then Redis Labs)
subcategory: in-memory database / cache
forks: Valkey (from Redis 7.2.4, BSD-3-Clause), announced 2024-03-28 under the Linux Foundation
key_takeaway: Redis shows the limits of relicensing when the hyperscalers are your biggest distribution channel: the moment the core closed, they forked it into a neutral foundation and made the fork their default. Redis Inc. still grew past $300M ARR, but it has not IPO'd and secondary markets value it below its 2021 $2B round. The reversal to AGPL after antirez returned suggests the company concluded that the open-source label mattered more for developer adoption than the licence protection did.

name: Sentry (Functional Software, Inc.)
subcategory: application error monitoring / observability
key_takeaway: Sentry is the architect of the 'delayed open source' middle ground: source-available now, Apache/MIT after two years, paired with direct payments to open-source maintainers ($1M in 2026). It is a third path between OSI licensing and permanent source-available licences, built for a company whose product is mainly consumed as a service.

name: Tiger Data (Timescale, Inc. d/b/a Tiger Data)
subcategory: time-series and analytics database (PostgreSQL extension)
key_takeaway: Tiger Data shows the 'extension' strategy: build on a community-governed open project (PostgreSQL), keep the core OSI-licensed, and restrict only cloud resale of add-ons. It avoided the fork dynamics of Elastic and Redis and reached unicorn status in 2022, then rebranded as Tiger Data in June 2025; no newer valuation was confirmed.

name: Airbyte, Inc.
subcategory: data integration (ELT connectors)
key_takeaway: Airbyte is the fast-closing case in this group: born MIT in 2020, ELv2 by 2021, a $1.5B valuation the same year, and then a long gap without new priced funding while bigger rivals merged. Openness bought rapid adoption; restriction came early to fend off cloud resellers, and the company's fate now depends on monetizing the cloud product.

name: Anaconda, Inc.
subcategory: Python/R data-science distribution and package repository; enterprise AI platform
forks: conda-forge (community channel) and Miniforge are the usual alternatives
key_takeaway: Anaconda is a cautionary case for scientific software: a company built on community open-source (NumPy/SciPy lineage) monetized by restricting access to the convenience layer (repository and installer) rather than the code, which shifted costs onto universities. Its 2025 raise at $1.5B and 2026 AI acquisitions show investors now value it as an enterprise AI platform rather than as a science tool.

name: Astronomer, Inc.
subcategory: data orchestration (managed Apache Airflow)
key_takeaway: Astronomer is the archetype of a founder startup commercializing a corporate-donated, foundation-governed project (Airbnb to ASF): it cannot capture the project via licensing, so it sells hosting and expertise against hyperscaler competition. Its 2025 crisis was reputational (a CEO scandal), not licence-related, and the company survived it.

name: Automattic Inc.
subcategory: web publishing (WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Jetpack, Tumblr)
key_takeaway: Automattic shows that a fully GPL product with weak neutral governance can turn a free-rider complaint into a governance crisis: the code stayed open, but the steward used trademarks and the plugin directory as leverage, leading to litigation (2024-2025) and a 2026 boardroom fight. Openness built a $7.5B (2021) company; personal control of the commons put it at risk.

name: Canonical Group Limited
subcategory: Linux distribution (Ubuntu) / support subscriptions
key_takeaway: Canonical shows that fully open software can win enormous adoption (Ubuntu) while capturing comparatively little revenue; independence was possible only because a wealthy founder absorbed years of losses. It is now a profitable, growing, founder-owned firm (~$345M revenue 2025) with no market valuation, illustrating a 'patient capital' path that VC-backed open-source firms rarely get.

name: Dagster Labs, Inc. (formerly Elementl)
subcategory: data orchestration (asset-based)
key_takeaway: Dagster shows the typical end-state for a well-liked but sub-scale open-core tool in a crowded category: no relicensing drama, modest funding, then acquisition by a competitor that keeps the open project alive. Openness protected users' continuity even though investors likely saw a limited return.

name: Databricks, Inc.
subcategory: data lakehouse / data + AI platform
key_takeaway: Databricks is the strongest case for the academic-spin-out, foundation-governed open-core model: the founders gave Spark to the ASF, kept the commercial value in a managed cloud service, and became the most valuable company in this group (~$190B, Aug 2026) without ever relicensing to a restrictive licence. AI demand, not the open-source projects alone, explains the 2025-2026 valuation surge.

name: dbt Labs, Inc. (formerly Fishtown Analytics; now 'Fivetran + dbt Labs')
subcategory: analytics engineering / SQL data transformation
key_takeaway: dbt Labs turned a consultancy's open-source tool into an industry standard and a $4.2B (2022) valuation, then consolidated with Fivetran rather than IPO. It shows how a permissive, community-defined standard can create large value for the ecosystem while the originating company's standalone outcome is merger rather than independence.

name: GitHub, Inc.
subcategory: code hosting / developer platform / AI coding (Copilot)
key_takeaway: GitHub is the clearest case of a closed platform built on top of the open-source commons: openness in the ecosystem, not in the product, generated its value, and AI (Copilot) became its growth engine after acquisition. Its 2025 absorption into Microsoft CoreAI shows the commons' central infrastructure is now controlled by a big-tech AI strategy.

name: GitLab Inc.
subcategory: DevOps / DevSecOps platform
key_takeaway: GitLab is a successful example of a community open-source project turned into a public open-core company. It moved from fully open (level 3) to open core (level 2) early and transparently, avoided licence controversies like those of database vendors, and reached ~$1B ARR, yet still competes mainly against a closed, Microsoft-backed rival and remains GAAP-unprofitable.

name: Hugging Face, Inc.
subcategory: open ML model/dataset hub and libraries
key_takeaway: Hugging Face is the strongest evidence in this group that openness can create outsized market value in the AI era: a small, open-core company became the commons' infrastructure and sold to Nvidia for $12.93B (Sep 2026). The trade-off is governance: the open AI ecosystem's main hub is moving from an independent startup to the dominant hardware vendor.

name: Mozilla Corporation
subcategory: web browser (Firefox) and consumer privacy products
key_takeaway: Mozilla is the archetype of maximum openness (level 4) with a non-profit parent: it cannot be bought or relicensed, and it has lasted 20+ years, yet its survival depends on payments from a dominant rival and on antitrust remedies. Openness guaranteed the mission's robustness but not financial independence.

name: MuleSoft, LLC (formerly MuleSource; owned by Salesforce)
subcategory: integration platform / API management (iPaaS)
key_takeaway: MuleSoft is the 'open-source on-ramp' case: a community project (2003) became open core, then a proprietary platform that IPO'd (2017) and sold to Salesforce for $6.5B (2018). The open edition was archived in 2026, illustrating how openness can fade once a big-company parent controls the product.

name: NGINX, Inc. (acquired by F5)
subcategory: web server / reverse proxy / load balancer
key_takeaway: NGINX shows the 'ubiquitous but under-monetized' pattern: the most-used web server earned its company a modest exit, and corporate stewardship under F5 led core developers to fork (freenginx, Angie). Openness made the code robust against both the Rambler ownership claim and F5's priorities, but not the company's independence.

name: Pivotal Software, Inc. and SpringSource (Interface21)
subcategory: enterprise Java framework (Spring) and cloud application platform (Cloud Foundry)
key_takeaway: Pivotal/SpringSource shows a corporate spin-out built from open-source assets: strong open projects (Spring, Cloud Foundry) did not make a durable standalone company, and the corporate parent reabsorbed it. Openness made the software outlive every owner change, from Interface21 to Broadcom.

name: Posit PBC (formerly RStudio, PBC)
subcategory: data-science IDEs and publishing tools (R and Python)
key_takeaway: Posit is the model of a mission-locked open-core company: a founder-led firm that converted to a public benefit corporation, spends about a third of engineering on open source, and sells enterprise deployment tools. It trades fast growth and a big valuation for longevity and community trust, which suits science users.

name: PostHog, Inc.
subcategory: product analytics / all-in-one product platform
key_takeaway: PostHog is a capital-efficient open-core startup: about $194M raised, profitable on cash flow, and valued at ~$1.4B (Oct 2025) within six years, with an MIT core and a fully FOSS mirror. It shows that clear separation of open and proprietary code (ee/ directory, posthog-foss) can avoid licence controversy while the business shifts to SaaS.

name: Prefect Technologies, Inc.
subcategory: workflow orchestration (Python) / agentic orchestration
key_takeaway: Prefect illustrates the 'second-generation open-core' pattern in data tooling: permissive licence, a hosted cloud for revenue, and a 2026 consolidation move (buying Dagster) plus a pivot to AI agent orchestration (FastMCP). Its financial size is opaque, so conclusions about value are weak.

name: Puppet, Inc. (formerly Puppet Labs; owned by Perforce)
subcategory: infrastructure configuration management / DevOps automation
key_takeaway: Puppet follows the post-acquisition closing pattern: a once-leading open-source DevOps tool, bought by a consolidator, then restricted (EULA-gated binaries, 25-node limit) in 2025, prompting a community fork (OpenVox) that research institutions adopted. Ownership change, not the founders, drove the closing.

name: Red Hat, Inc.
subcategory: enterprise Linux / hybrid cloud platform
forks: OpenELA (Open Enterprise Linux Association); Rocky Linux; AlmaLinux
key_takeaway: Red Hat is the canonical proof that a pure open-source (level 3) business can reach large scale, longevity (30+ years) and a top-tier exit. Its later history shows the main risk of that model is not competitors closing the code but downstream clones freely reusing it; Red Hat's answer was to restrict distribution channels rather than relicense, keeping OSI licences while tightening control, and post-acquisition integration into IBM is now the main threat to its independent culture.

name: Supabase, Inc.
subcategory: Postgres development platform / backend-as-a-service
key_takeaway: Supabase is the clearest AI-era counterexample to relicensing: a level-3, Apache-2.0 company that grew from founding (2020) to a $10B pre-money valuation (Jun 2026) by being the open, Postgres-based backend that AI coding tools default to. Its risk is concentration on the AI app boom, not openness.

name: SUSE S.A.
subcategory: enterprise Linux / Kubernetes (Rancher)
key_takeaway: SUSE shows that a fully open-source vendor can survive 30+ years and many owners because customers and the community depend on the code, not the cap table; but being the second open vendor in a market tends to yield modest growth, PE ownership, and periodic cost-cutting rather than a large standalone valuation.

name: Vercel Inc. (formerly ZEIT)
subcategory: frontend cloud / web hosting (Next.js) and AI app tooling (v0, AI SDK)
key_takeaway: Vercel is the 'framework-as-funnel' model: give away the dominant React framework, sell the managed cloud that runs it best, and ride the AI app wave ($9.3B, Sep 2025). Openness here strengthened market value; the main risks are security incidents and reputation, not licensing.

name: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2)
subcategory: non-profit AI research; fully open LLMs (OLMo), open training data (Dolma), Semantic Scholar
key_takeaway: Ai2 is the 'fully open' benchmark in the study: weights, data, code, checkpoints and logs released under Apache-2.0 by a non-profit with no product to protect. It shows what open science in AI looks like when the licence and the data are both open, and that governments (NSF) will fund it for scientific use. Its weakness is money, not openness, so its relevance depends on continued philanthropic and public funding rather than market value.

name: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (Qwen / Tongyi Qianwen)
subcategory: e-commerce and cloud (Alibaba Cloud); Qwen open-weights and proprietary LLMs (non-US comparator)
key_takeaway: Alibaba's Qwen is the non-US mirror of Meta's Llama strategy, but with a more permissive licence: Apache-2.0 open weights for most sizes made Qwen a widely used base model in the open ecosystem (200,000+ variants), while frontier 'Max' models and cloud services earn the money. Its 2026 revenue-threshold licence for the largest model shows the same drift as US firms toward restricting the top tier. For the study, Qwen shows that permissive licensing can win global adoption even under geopolitical headwinds, though not market-value gains (shares fell 42% in a year).

name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
subcategory: search / advertising / cloud; AI models (Gemini closed, Gemma open) and developer platforms (Android, Chromium, Kubernetes, TensorFlow)
key_takeaway: Alphabet is a selective opener: it open-sources platforms and infrastructure that widen the market for its paid services, and hands some (Kubernetes) to neutral foundations, but holds the frontier AI and the distribution chokepoints itself. Android shows that an open-source licence alone does not guarantee openness: the code is still Apache-2.0, yet in-house development, sparse source drops and developer verification have moved real control back to Google. Gemma's 2026 move to Apache-2.0 suggests the open-weights tier has become a competitive commodity in which restrictive custom licences no l

name: Amazon.com, Inc. (Amazon Web Services)
subcategory: e-commerce and cloud (AWS); large consumer of open-source software, maintainer of forks (OpenSearch, Valkey) and of Firecracker
key_takeaway: Amazon is the counterweight in the open-source economy: the cloud host whose resale of open projects triggered the move to source-available licences, and which then turned into a foundation-backed open-source sponsor to keep those projects permissive. Its own differentiating assets (AWS services, Nova models) remain proprietary. For the study, AWS shows that a deep-pocketed host can neutralise a single vendor's relicensing by forking into a foundation, so the vendor's closing yields less protection than intended.

name: Anthropic, PBC
subcategory: frontier LLMs (Claude, closed weights); open standards and tools (Model Context Protocol, interpretability tooling)
key_takeaway: Anthropic is the 'closed model, open standards' strategy: it keeps the frontier models proprietary on safety and commercial grounds while open-sourcing the interfaces (MCP) and the science of understanding models (interpretability tools), then putting the most important of these under neutral governance. That combination earned it the network effects of a standard without the competitive exposure of open weights. For the study, it shows that openness at the protocol layer can be strategically decisive even for a lab that releases no model weights.

name: Apple Inc.
subcategory: consumer hardware and platforms (iPhone, Mac, iOS/macOS); on-device AI (Apple Intelligence)
key_takeaway: Apple is the control case for the study: the least open of the big platforms in AI and developer tooling, and the most valuable. Openness at Apple is tactical and peripheral (Swift, MLX, small OpenELM models under a non-OSI licence), and even its open OS core has become less visible over time. Its 2026 reliance on Google's Gemini suggests that a closed strategy without frontier models of its own leaves it buying from rivals, a different risk from that faced by open-ecosystem players.

name: DeepSeek
subcategory: frontier open-weights LLMs (V3/V4, R1) and low-cost API
key_takeaway: DeepSeek is the strongest evidence in this group that open weights can shift market structure: an MIT-licensed model from a 2023 hedge-fund spin-off moved hundreds of billions in market value, prompted Sam Altman to say OpenAI needed 'a different open source strategy' (Jan 2025), before its Apache-2.0 gpt-oss release (Aug 2025), and fed Meta's rethink and still produced a $52-70B private valuation. Its openness is about weights and licence, not data, and its biggest risks are geopolitical rather than commercial. For the study, it shows that a permissive licence can be a competitive weapon for

name: EleutherAI (EleutherAI Institute)
subcategory: grassroots, then non-profit, open AI research: open LLMs (GPT-Neo/J/NeoX, Pythia), datasets (The Pile, Common Pile), evaluation tools
key_takeaway: EleutherAI is the community-origin case: openness was its entire reason for existing, and it converted into a non-profit institute rather than a company. It shows that open AI science can be produced at low cost by volunteers with donated compute, that open data carries legal risk that full transparency makes visible, and that the fix is better-licensed data rather than closing. For the study, it is a pure public-goods producer whose value appears in downstream adoption, not in a valuation.

name: Google DeepMind, AI for Science (AlphaFold) and Isomorphic Labs
subcategory: AI for science: protein structure (AlphaFold), materials (GNoME), genomics (AlphaGenome); drug-discovery spin-out Isomorphic Labs
forks: Open reimplementations: Protenix (ByteDance, Apache-2.0), OpenFold-3 (AlQuraishi lab, MIT), Boltz-1/2 (MIT)
key_takeaway: AlphaFold is the cleanest natural experiment in the study: the fully open version (AF2 plus the EMBL-EBI database) produced enormous scientific impact and prestige, while the restricted successor (AF3) mainly spurred open clones and a well-funded proprietary spin-out. For physical-science labs, it shows that open science infrastructure gets adopted fastest when data and weights are under CC-BY/Apache terms and co-hosted by a public institution, and that a corporate owner will close the next generation once a commercial route (drug discovery) appears.

name: International Business Machines Corporation (IBM)
subcategory: enterprise software, hybrid cloud, consulting, mainframes; acquirer of open-source companies (Red Hat, HashiCorp, Confluent); Granite open models
key_takeaway: IBM is the open-source acquirer: having been a proprietary vendor for most of its history, it now buys the companies that monetise open communities (Linux, Terraform, Kafka) and releases its own AI models under Apache-2.0. The market has not rewarded the strategy as richly as the AI-centric giants (about $220B market cap, down ~21% in a year). For the study, IBM shows that openness can be bought as a revenue stream, and that licence closures made before an acquisition (HashiCorp) carry their forks along with them.

name: Meta Platforms, Inc. (formerly Facebook, Inc.)
subcategory: social media / advertising; AI models (Llama, Muse) and developer frameworks (PyTorch, React)
key_takeaway: Meta is the clearest example of commoditize-your-complement openness in AI: its money comes from advertising, so giving away frameworks and model weights cost little and undercut rivals whose business is selling model access. The record splits in two. Developer infrastructure was open-sourced and then put under neutral governance, which makes it robust. Model weights stayed under Meta's own non-OSI licence and were the first thing to close once the strategy changed. For the study, Meta shows that licence and governance, not the label 'open source', decide whether openness survives a change of

name: Microsoft Corporation
subcategory: software / cloud (Azure, Microsoft 365); developer platforms (.NET, VS Code, TypeScript, GitHub); AI (OpenAI partnership, Phi open models)
key_takeaway: Microsoft is the canonical convert: once its revenue moved from selling Windows licences to renting cloud capacity, open source changed from threat to on-ramp, and it open-sourced its developer stack and bought the platform where open source lives. Its openness is real at the tool and small-model layer and absent at the money-making core, an open-core strategy run at the scale of a $3.6T company. For the study it shows that a firm's stance on openness tracks where its profits come from, not ideology.

name: Mistral AI SAS
subcategory: LLMs: open-weights (Apache-2.0) plus proprietary premier models, API and Le Chat
key_takeaway: Mistral is the open-core AI lab: it uses Apache-2.0 releases for reach and sovereignty credentials, and keeps some premier models closed or under custom licences for revenue. Its licence history oscillates (open, then partly closed in 2024, then broadly open again in 2025-26), which shows that for AI labs openness is a competitive setting rather than a fixed identity. For the study, it is the best non-US example of openness used to build a high-valuation challenger quickly.

name: NVIDIA Corporation
subcategory: GPUs and accelerated computing; CUDA software platform; Nemotron open models
key_takeaway: NVIDIA is the complement that profits whenever models are open: the more labs and companies train and run open-weights models, the more GPUs they buy, so NVIDIA now funds one of the most transparent open-model programmes (weights, data, recipes) while keeping CUDA closed. Its openness is therefore strategic and layered: open at the edges and in models, closed at the software platform that locks in its hardware. For the study, NVIDIA shows that a closed platform can coexist with, and benefit from, open science built on top of it.

name: OpenAI (OpenAI Foundation; OpenAI Group PBC)
subcategory: frontier LLMs (GPT), ChatGPT and API; occasional open-weights releases (GPT-2, gpt-oss)
key_takeaway: OpenAI is the archetype of an organisation founded on openness that became closed as its models became valuable. Its name and 2015 pledge to publish code now sit beside an $852B closed-model business, and its one major re-opening (gpt-oss under Apache-2.0) was a response to open-weights competitors rather than a return to its founding model. For the study, it is the clearest example of openness used to launch, then traded for control once capital needs rose, with governance (a non-profit holding special voting rights) kept as the remaining link to the original mission.

name: Oracle Corporation
subcategory: database, enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure (OCI); steward of Java/OpenJDK and MySQL via the Sun acquisition
forks: Jenkins; LibreOffice (The Document Foundation); illumos (2010); OpenIndiana (launched 2010-09-14)
key_takeaway: Oracle shows what happens when a proprietary-minded owner acquires open-source assets: the communities fork and the lasting value walks out (MariaDB, LibreOffice, Jenkins, illumos), while the owner keeps the trademarks and a smaller share of the ecosystem. Its AI strategy is pure infrastructure for closed labs, which has made it a leveraged bet on OpenAI rather than a participant in open AI. For the study, Oracle is the clearest closing case among the incumbents, and the forks are the evidence that open licences protect users against a hostile steward.

name: Stability AI Ltd
subcategory: generative image, video, audio and 3D models (Stable Diffusion family)
key_takeaway: Stability AI is the cautionary case: open weights won adoption and mindshare almost overnight, but without a paid product or a deep-pocketed parent, openness turned into cost and legal exposure, followed by a cash crisis, a founder exit and a tighter licence. For the study, it shows that open model releases are sustainable for companies that monetise something else (Meta, NVIDIA, cloud providers) or are funded as public goods (Ai2, EleutherAI), and precarious for startups whose only asset is the model.

name: xAI (X.AI Holdings Corp.; subsidiary of SpaceX since Feb 2026)
subcategory: frontier LLMs (Grok) and consumer chatbot integrated with X
key_takeaway: xAI is the 'open-washing' contrast case: its founder sued OpenAI over abandoning its non-profit founding mission (Musk v. Altman, lost May 2026; see openai.json), yet xAI is closed at the frontier, releasing older weights under a licence that blocks the most valuable reuse (training other models). Its trajectory from 2023 founding to a $250B acquisition price shows that a frontier lab's market value can be built almost entirely without openness. For the study, it shows why the licence of an open-weights release matters as much as the release itself.

name: Adafruit Industries, LLC
subcategory: maker electronics: open-source boards, sensors, kits, CircuitPython, tutorials and retail
key_takeaway: Adafruit is the bootstrapped open-hardware model. It is founder-owned, has taken no funding on record, and has operated for 21 years in New York. It publishes CC BY-SA design files and holds more OSHWA certifications (about 413 by 2020) than any other firm studied here. Its scale is modest: the last disclosed revenue was about $45M in 2016, with about 105 staff. It shows open hardware can be durable and profitable without venture capital, by selling convenience, curation and education around designs anyone may copy. The trade-off is that it stays small and private, with no recorded valuation.

name: Arduino (Arduino S.r.l. / Arduino LLC; Qualcomm deal announced 2025)
subcategory: microcontroller boards, IDE and cloud for makers, education and industry
key_takeaway: Arduino is the canonical open-hardware success whose value went mostly to the ecosystem and to clone makers rather than to the company. The path runs from academic origin (2005), through a trademark fight that split the brand (2008-2016) and a founder buyback (2017), to modest venture funding ($54M, 2022-2023). It ends in consolidation into a chip vendor: Qualcomm, announced Oct 2025, price undisclosed, closing not confirmed by a primary source here. The published designs have so far stayed open, but the post-announcement Terms of Service (Oct 2025) tightened control of the cloud platform and

name: Bambu Lab (Shenzhen Tuozhu Technology)
subcategory: consumer/prosumer FFF 3D printers (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Bambu Lab is the closed comparator that won: a DJI-alumni, VC-backed (IDG Capital) Shenzhen firm that reused open slicer code, kept printers and firmware proprietary, and in January 2025 tightened control further with authorization firmware, accepting a community backlash. Its rise is the main competitive force behind open pioneers' retreat (Prusa) and shows the 'open software, closed hardware' pattern at its most commercially effective.

name: Creality (Shenzhen Creality 3D Technology Co., Ltd.)
subcategory: consumer FFF and resin 3D printers, scanners and laser engravers
key_takeaway: Creality is the volume-oriented Chinese counterpart to Prusa's story: it began closed and GPL-noncompliant, opened one hit design (Ender-3, 2018) and later its Klipper firmware, and used that openness to fuel a huge modding community while keeping newer hardware proprietary, reaching a Hong Kong listing in 2026. Openness here worked as a marketing and ecosystem tool for a low-cost manufacturer rather than as a core principle.

name: Formlabs Inc.
subcategory: professional SLA/SLS 3D printers and materials (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Formlabs is the US closed comparator that scaled: an MIT Media Lab spin-out with about $249M in disclosed venture rounds, a $2B 2021 valuation, about $250M 2025 revenue and 750 staff, larger than every open desktop-printer maker in this group. It suggests that in professional additive manufacturing, proprietary integration of printer, materials and software captured more value than open designs did, with selective interface openness used as a growth tool.

name: Framework Computer Inc.
subcategory: repairable, modular laptops and desktops
key_takeaway: Framework is a US example of partial, interface-level openness as a business strategy: publish the module interfaces, CAD and EC firmware so customers and third parties can repair and extend the machine, but keep the mainboard design and BIOS proprietary. It sits at level 2 and shows that 'open where it builds an ecosystem, closed where it protects the core' can sustain a VC-backed hardware startup through 2026, with firmware update cadence as the main weakness.

name: LulzBot (Aleph Objects, Inc.; since 2019 FAME 3D LLC)
subcategory: desktop FFF 3D printers (free/libre hardware)
key_takeaway: LulzBot is the purest test of fully free hardware as a business: it reached Inc. 5000-scale revenue but collapsed in 2019 for ordinary cash-flow reasons, and its open designs then let a regional manufacturer (FAME 3D) revive the line, which still publishes GPL source for current printers in 2026. Openness neither caused nor prevented the failure; it made the product line resilient to the company's death.

name: MakerBot Industries, LLC
subcategory: desktop FFF 3D printers (now UltiMaker's education brand)
key_takeaway: MakerBot is the canonical 'open, then closed, then absorbed' arc: openness and community created the brand and the exit value, and closing (just before the Stratasys deal) traded community goodwill for proprietary control that did not prevent rapid value destruction. Within seven years of the $403M deal it was folded into Ultimaker as a minority-owned brand.

name: Open Compute Project Foundation
subcategory: open data-centre hardware specifications consortium
key_takeaway: OCP is the buyer-led model of open hardware: the largest customers publish designs so that many manufacturers compete to build them, and a foundation keeps the specs neutral. It shows open hardware can reach a market measured in hundreds of billions of dollars of spending when demand is concentrated in a few giant buyers, while the value accrues to those buyers and to vendors rather than to any open-hardware company. Market figures are forecasts commissioned by OCP itself and measure spending on 'OCP-recognized' equipment, not OCP revenue.

name: OpenBCI
subcategory: open-source biosensing / brain-computer interface (EEG) hardware
key_takeaway: OpenBCI is the open-science hardware archetype: a crowdfunded (2013) Brooklyn startup whose open EEG boards and GPL-licensed 3D-printable headset made research-grade biosensing affordable. It has stayed small and private, and its recent focus is a premium, apparently closed multimodal headset (Galea) for XR and defence-adjacent markets. Openness created the research user base. Whether it also funds the company could not be determined, because no funding or revenue figures were reachable without search.

name: Oxide Computer Company
subcategory: rack-scale on-premises cloud computers
key_takeaway: Oxide is the 'open firmware, closed boards' pattern at rack scale: everything from the service-processor OS to the control plane is MPL-2.0 on GitHub, but revenue comes from selling proprietary integrated racks. It is a US example of a long, capital-heavy hardware build-out (four years to first product) that by 2026 reported taxable profit and backlog-driven fundraising, and it builds directly on the Open Compute Project's open rack ideas.

name: Pine64 (Pine Store Limited)
subcategory: community-oriented ARM/RISC-V single-board computers, laptops, phones and wearables
key_takeaway: Pine64 is the 'community supplies the software, company supplies cheap hardware' model: openness lives mostly in community-maintained software, while hardware is documented (schematics, now 3D files) but not openly licensed. Founded in California and moved to Hong Kong in 2019-2020, it has survived a decade on crowdfunding and sales rather than VC, at small scale.

name: Prusa Research a.s.
subcategory: desktop FFF 3D printers
key_takeaway: Prusa is the clearest case of an open-hardware pioneer retreating to 'open software, source-available hardware': it kept firmware (GPL) and slicer (AGPL) open but moved its newest printers' CAD to a custom non-commercial Open Community License. Openness built the brand and community cheaply, but it did not protect against well-funded closed competitors, and the protective licence came after market share had already shifted.

name: Raspberry Pi Holdings plc (and the Raspberry Pi Foundation)
subcategory: single-board computers and microcontrollers (RP2040/RP2350)
key_takeaway: Raspberry Pi is the clearest success of 'open software, closed hardware' in this group. A charity founded it, it went public in 2024 at about $689M, and it was worth about $1.19B on 2026-11-23, profitable on hardware sales alone. Openness sits in the OS, drivers and microcontroller SDK. The SoC, boot firmware and board designs stay proprietary and single-sourced from Broadcom and Sony, which protects margins but leaves the platform dependent on one vendor. Foundation ownership locks in the mission but is being diluted by share sales. For the study it is the counterexample to the idea that the

name: RepRap project
subcategory: self-replicating open-source FFF 3D printer project
key_takeaway: RepRap is the open-hardware 'commons' baseline: an academic, grant-funded, GPL project with community governance that created an industry (MakerBot, Prusa, Ultimaker, LulzBot all descend from it) while capturing almost none of the money. It shows the time pattern clearly: enormous early diffusion, then commercial descendants closing up as markets matured, with the commons surviving as knowledge rather than as an organization.

name: RISC-V International (formerly RISC-V Foundation)
subcategory: open instruction-set architecture standards body
key_takeaway: RISC-V International shows the 'open standard, closed products' division of labour in hardware: a lean nonprofit (about $8.6M revenue in 2024) maintains a fully open, royalty-free specification while companies compete with proprietary implementations on top. It is the most robust governance form in this group, and its main risks are geopolitical rather than commercial.

name: Seeed Technology Co., Ltd. (Seeed Studio)
subcategory: open-source hardware modules and dev boards (XIAO), edge-AI devices (reCamera), PCB/PCBA manufacturing (Seeed Fusion)
key_takeaway: Seeed is the Shenzhen counterpart to Adafruit and SparkFun: an open-hardware-first company that also sells manufacturing services and runs maker community infrastructure. It has lasted 18 years. Its competitive edge comes from Shenzhen supply-chain scale rather than design exclusivity or patents, so open design files cost it little. Its openness is real but informal: files are published, licences are often missing, and it holds no OSHWA certifications. The pages reachable without search gave no funding, revenue or valuation figures, so its size relative to its US peers is unknown here.

name: SiFive, Inc.
subcategory: RISC-V processor IP and fabless semiconductor
key_takeaway: SiFive is the clearest example of open-standard, closed-implementation hardware: the open RISC-V ISA created the market, while SiFive's own open-source platform was archived once it had served as a launch vehicle. It shows that an open specification can support a multi-billion-dollar US company, but the money comes from proprietary IP, long timelines and repeated large VC rounds, not from selling open designs.

name: Sofar Ocean Technologies (formerly OpenROV)
subcategory: ocean sensing: open-source ROV kits (OpenROV), then Spotter buoy network, marine weather and voyage-optimization software
key_takeaway: Sofar/OpenROV traces the full arc from open-hardware DIY project to closed, VC-backed data company. It began in 2011 with public CAD under a non-commercial CC licence and a community in 30+ countries. The 2019 merger made it a business of Spotter buoys and data software sold to shipping and the Navy. It closed the product and later opened a standard (Bristlemouth) where interoperability serves it, the 'open the interfaces, close the product' pattern. Its CC BY-NC-SA licence also shows a common open-science compromise that does not meet the OSHW definition. Funding after the 2019 $7M Series A,

name: SparkFun Electronics
subcategory: maker electronics: open-source development and breakout boards, kits, education
key_takeaway: SparkFun is the long-lived, mid-sized open-hardware manufacturer. It was founded by a student in 2003 and still operates from Colorado, publishing schematics and EAGLE files for 400+ in-house designs, with an explicit no-patents policy and an early role in writing the OSHW definition. No valuation, funding or revenue is public, and no recent headcount was found beyond about 140 in 2018. It supports the pattern that open hardware firms can be durable but stay small and private. The trademark and trade-dress disputes (SPARC 2009-2010, Fluke 2014) show that brand, not design IP, is where open-har

name: System76, Inc.
subcategory: Linux computers, open firmware and open-hardware peripherals
key_takeaway: System76 is a long-lived US example of an open-software-first hardware company that opened progressively, ending up with open OS, open firmware and some fully open hardware (Launch, OSHWA US001062), while its laptops remain closed ODM designs. Its longevity (since 2005) without disclosed outside funding contrasts with VC-backed peers, though its ownership and finances are not public.

name: UltiMaker (Ultimaker B.V.)
subcategory: desktop and professional FFF 3D printers; Cura slicer
key_takeaway: UltiMaker is the 'open slicer, closed printers' pattern from the European side: its RepRap-community origins and non-commercially licensed early designs gave way to proprietary professional printers, while LGPL Cura became the ecosystem anchor. Consolidation (the 2022 MakerBot merger under NPM Capital) rather than openness determined its corporate path.

name: Atinary Technologies
subcategory: no-code AI/ML experiment-optimization platform (SDLabs) and 'Self-Driving Labs(R)'
key_takeaway: Atinary is the closed 'SDL brain' vendor. Its founders have worked on AI-driven R&D since 2017, coined and trademarked 'Self-Driving Labs', and sell no-code optimization SaaS that plugs into Chemspeed, Bruker, ABB and others. Its 2026 Boston lab and Bruker collaboration show lab-automation incumbents assembling proprietary end-to-end SDL stacks. That contrasts with the open-source optimizers and orchestration tools common in academic SDLs, which Atinary does not contribute to.

name: Benchling, Inc.
subcategory: cloud R&D informatics SaaS (ELN, molecular biology, registry, LIMS) for biotech
key_takeaway: Benchling is the closed-SaaS benchmark for lab software. It is founder-led (MIT/YC 2012), raised about $406M, was valued at $6.1B at the 2021 peak and has about 810 employees. It has never open-sourced its product, and its free academic tier did the community-building job that open source does for others. The lack of any public valuation, IPO or reported down round since 2021 makes its current value unknown. Fetched sources could not confirm 2023-2026 restructuring.

name: Chemify Ltd
subcategory: chemputation: programmable robotic chemical synthesis + AI ('hyperscaler for chemistry')
key_takeaway: Chemify is the academic-spinout version of the AI-plus-automation chemistry company: a decade of Glasgow research on programmable chemistry (Chemputer, XDL, partly public on GitHub) has become a proprietary 'hyperscaler for chemistry'. By late 2026 it had at least $93M in equity plus GBP 22M of UK public grants, and a Chemifarm facility opened in 2025. Public and academic investment created the paradigm; the commercial asset is closed.

name: Chemspeed Technologies AG
subcategory: automated synthesis, formulation and gravimetric powder-dosing workstations for chemistry and materials labs
key_takeaway: Chemspeed is the closed-hardware counterpart to Opentrons. It is a long-lived Swiss maker of solid- and liquid-handling synthesis robots, widely used in chemistry and materials SDLs, never open, and absorbed by Bruker in 2024. Its exit was a quiet strategic acquisition, not venture hype. It now anchors a closed Bruker-Chemspeed-Atinary SDL stack (Aug 2026 collaboration), illustrating consolidation of lab automation into incumbents' proprietary ecosystems.

name: Citrine Informatics, Inc.
subcategory: materials informatics SaaS (AI for materials and chemicals R&D)
key_takeaway: Citrine is the incumbent US materials-informatics startup, founded in 2013. It shows the slow, capital-light path: about $52M or more in announced rounds over a decade, real industrial customers and grants, and peripheral open tooling (Apache-2.0 SDK, data model, ML library) around a closed SaaS core. By 2025-2026 it was dwarfed in funding by closed AI-for-materials newcomers (Periodic Labs' $300M seed, CuspAI's >$650M), and responded by rebranding around 'industrial superintelligence' rather than opening up.

name: CuspAI (Cusp AI Limited)
subcategory: AI materials-discovery platform ('AI Materials Foundry') for semiconductors, energy and chemicals
key_takeaway: CuspAI, Cambridge UK, founded 2024 by Chad Edwards and Max Welling, had raised over $650M by late 2026, among the largest sums in AI for materials. It has released nothing open, and its edge is a partner ecosystem combining licensed crystallographic databases, Wiley literature, semiconductor and chemicals companies and Meta's open models. It is the archetype of consuming open and licensed scientific data while keeping outputs proprietary.

name: Emerald Cloud Lab, Inc.
subcategory: cloud lab (remotely programmed, centralized automated wet lab as a subscription service)
key_takeaway: Emerald Cloud Lab is the surviving US closed cloud lab. It sells subscription access to a centralized robotic facility and has opened only its programming layer, for research use under an unnamed licence. Its biggest strategic wins, the $40M Carnegie Mellon university cloud lab and the NSF GEMSTONE node, came through academic partners that asked for open standards and data. So the open parts of the ECL ecosystem are increasingly paid for by universities and NSF, while the facility, scheduling software and operations stay proprietary.

name: EvolutionaryScale, PBC
subcategory: protein language / generative biology foundation models (ESM3, ESM C)
key_takeaway: EvolutionaryScale is the counter-example to 'start open, then close'. It began as a Meta FAIR open-science project (ESM), raised a $142M seed as a company with non-commercial open weights, and within about two years was folded into the non-profit Biohub, where its open models moved to MIT. For the study it suggests that frontier scientific foundation models may find a more stable home in philanthropic or non-profit structures than in VC-backed API businesses. Its timeline (relicence date, deal terms) still needs confirming.

name: Isomorphic Labs Limited
subcategory: AI drug discovery (Alphabet spin-off of Google DeepMind)
key_takeaway: Isomorphic Labs is the clearest case of 'open public data in, closed models out'. AlphaFold was trained on the PDB, a decades-old open archive. Its open AlphaFold 2 and DB won a Nobel and built trust, yet the commercial successor (AF3, IsoDDE) ships with non-commercial weights or not at all. Investor appetite for that closed position is enormous: $600M in 2025, then $2.1B and $5B in 2026, the largest AI-for-science financing in this group, still with no clinical asset.

name: Kebotix, Inc.
subcategory: AI + robotic self-driving lab for materials and chemicals discovery
key_takeaway: Kebotix was an early (c. 2017-2022) closed AI-plus-robotics materials-discovery startup with strong recognition (C&EN, WEF, MIT Tech Review) and blue-chip partners, but its public activity stops around 2022. Whether it 'shut down' is unconfirmed: the website is live with a 2026 copyright but has no news after ~Mar 2022. It is a cautionary early mover that predates the 2025-2026 funding wave and left no open artifacts.

name: Lila Sciences, Inc.
subcategory: 'scientific superintelligence' + autonomous AI Science Factories (life science, chemistry, materials, energy)
key_takeaway: Lila Sciences is the Flagship version of the 2025-2026 AI-for-science boom. It raised $550M in seven months of 2025, was valued above $1.3B with NVIDIA backing, and makes heavy physical-science claims (green-hydrogen catalysts, carbon-capture sorbents), all on proprietary instruments and data. It publishes papers but releases no models, data or code, so it shares results, not the means to reproduce them.

name: Opentrons Labworks, Inc.
subcategory: lab automation / low-cost liquid-handling robots
key_takeaway: Opentrons is the canonical open-hardware lab-automation test case, and its arc is 'open to enter, close the hardware to scale': the open OT-One won early users cheaply, but revenue came from a closed-hardware OT-2/Flex whose open Apache-2.0 API is the remaining open asset and the reason it dominates academic self-driving-lab builds. Its valuation fell about 91% from the 2021 SoftBank round to the 2025 Series D, a COVID boom-and-bust rather than a verdict on openness. In 2026 it repositioned as 'open, AI-native' infrastructure connecting AI to the wet lab, marketing 'open' as API access rather

name: Orbital Industries (formerly Orbital Materials)
subcategory: AI materials discovery -> 'AI Industrial' (CurieOS platform, data-centre cooling hardware)
key_takeaway: Orbital (Materials, now Industries) shows that an AI-for-materials startup can stay genuinely open at the model layer: Apache-2.0 Orb potentials trained on open DFT datasets such as OMol25. It still has to find revenue in closed products, here an agentic R&D platform licensed to BASF and PFAS-free GPU cooling for AI data centres. Openness bought reputation and community, not revenue, and the company's rebrand to an 'AI Industrial' signals where it expects the money.

name: Periodic Labs
subcategory: AI scientist + autonomous materials-synthesis labs (superconductors, magnets, heat shields)
key_takeaway: Periodic Labs is the clearest bet that physical-science AI value lies in closed, self-generated lab data. It raised $300M at founding, the largest round in this group for a pure materials-discovery startup, and its only public outputs a year later are blog posts and a claimed 1-trillion-parameter model it has not released. Its founders' previous work at Google and OpenAI built on and fed open materials science, yet Periodic itself returns nothing open. It is the reference point for a 'closed AI-for-materials' model.

name: Radical AI, Inc.
subcategory: AI + self-driving lab for materials (alloys, aerospace, hydrogen purification)
key_takeaway: Radical AI is the 2025 New York entrant pairing a proprietary alloy-discovery self-driving lab with an open-source simulation engine. It illustrates the dominant 2025-2026 pattern among AI-for-materials startups: open the commodity tooling (TorchSim), close the data and the discovered materials. Its funding ($55M seed+) is modest next to Periodic Labs and Lila, but government contracts give it a defense-materials niche.

name: Recursion Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
subcategory: AI-driven drug discovery ('TechBio'), automated phenomics data factory, clinical-stage
key_takeaway: Recursion is the public-market test of the 'automated lab plus AI' thesis. After 13 years and the Exscientia merger it has about $75M in revenue, a net loss of roughly $645M (2025) and a $1.66B market cap, below its 2021 IPO level. Its open-science activity (RxRx, OpenPhenom, Boltz-2) is real but deliberately peripheral: curated, mostly non-commercial releases of under 1% of its data, sometimes trained on public consortium data, while the data that matter stay proprietary. It anticipates the 'open papers and benchmarks, closed data' pattern of the 2025-2026 AI-for-science labs.

name: Schrödinger, Inc.
subcategory: physics-based molecular simulation software + drug discovery
key_takeaway: Schrödinger is the closed, physics-based, academically derived incumbent that AI-for-science entrants are measured against. It is 35 years old, public since 2020, earned $256M revenue in 2025 and sells to materials customers, yet it loses money and was worth about $1.8B in November 2026, below its end-2021 and end-2023 values. In 2025 it pulled back from running its own clinical trials toward software and partnering. That suggests its durable business is selling closed simulation tools, even as open academic engines cover parts of the same stack for free.

name: Strateos, Inc. (formerly Transcriptic)
subcategory: cloud lab (robotic remote lab for drug discovery), later private-lab software (LodeStar/SmartLab)
search_tool: WebSearch (+ WebFetch of cited pages); budget exhausted after 8 queries
key_takeaway: Strateos (ex-Transcriptic) is the cautionary tale among US cloud labs. Over a decade it raised roughly $80M+ in announced rounds, won Eli Lilly as an anchor partner, and opened only a peripheral protocol standard. In April 2023 it abandoned the hosted cloud-lab model for on-site private-lab consulting, and since then its web presence has gone stale and its ownership is unconfirmed. Its open Autoprotocol library outlived the business model but never achieved network effects, which suggests an open interface standard alone cannot rescue a capital-intensive, closed, centralized lab service.

name: Ansys, Inc. (now part of Synopsys)
subcategory: engineering simulation (FEA, CFD, electromagnetics)
key_takeaway: Ansys is the high-water mark for closed physical-science software value: a 1970 founder startup that became a $35B acquisition. Its trajectory (VC buyout, IPO, strategic sale to an EDA firm) is the commercial template against which open simulation infrastructure such as OpenFOAM and LAMMPS can be compared: far more capital captured, but control concentrated in a single owner.

name: The Apache Software Foundation (ASF)
subcategory: volunteer-run open-source software foundation (501(c)(3))
latest_value_type: annual revenue, IRS Form 990, fiscal year ending April 2025 (expenses $2,334,727)
key_takeaway: The ASF is the low-budget, high-legitimacy end of open governance: roughly $2.2M a year in revenue supports 290+ projects, about one-hundredth of the Linux Foundation's $221M. For science it is a reminder that foundation budgets measure overhead, not the value of what they steward.

name: COMSOL (COMSOL AB / COMSOL Group)
subcategory: multiphysics finite-element simulation
key_takeaway: COMSOL is the private, founder-controlled closed comparator: 40 years old, 700+ employees and still independent, but opaque (no revenue disclosed). For the study it represents closed software whose longevity comes from steady licence sales rather than an exit, with AI added as a feature on top of proprietary solvers.

name: DOE CODE (DOE Office of Scientific and Technical Information) and national-lab software release policy
subcategory: federal software registry, repository and DOI service for DOE-funded code
key_takeaway: DOE CODE quantifies the US government's open-source science output: about 5,900 inventoried releases since 2017, led by LLNL (826), PNNL (721), Sandia (698) and LBNL (641), 94% of them open source and mostly permissively licensed. It shows national labs default to openness once code is released, but its own data also show a recent slowdown and a stale public inventory.

name: Enthought, Inc.
subcategory: scientific Python software, consulting and R&D AI services
key_takeaway: Enthought is a case of an open-science-software pioneer that monetised through services and distributions, then pivoted to proprietary AI consulting for materials and chemistry R&D. It illustrates that seeding open infrastructure (SciPy) creates large public value that the originating company need not capture.

name: Gaussian, Inc.
subcategory: quantum chemistry (electronic structure) software
key_takeaway: Gaussian shows the sharpest governance risk of closed scientific software: the vendor can decide who may use, test and compare its code, and did so against competing method developers. It is long-lived and commercially stable at modest academic prices ($2,500 to $6,000 per US academic licence), but its licence terms, not its science, are what the community remembers.

name: Globus (University of Chicago)
subcategory: research data transfer, sharing and automation service (nonprofit SaaS)
key_takeaway: Globus is the freemium counter-model in open science infrastructure: a university-operated service that charges institutions for advanced features while keeping basic transfers free for non-profit researchers. It shows that 'open science' infrastructure can be sustained by subscriptions rather than grants, at the cost of open-source control.

name: The HDF Group
subcategory: scientific data format and library (HDF4, HDF5, HSDS)
latest_value_type: annual revenue, IRS Form 990, fiscal year ending Dec 2025 (92.6% program services, 0.4% contributions)
key_takeaway: The HDF Group shows the 'services nonprofit' model for academic-origin open infrastructure: 20 years independent of NCSA, but revenue has drifted down to about $3M and 17 staff while HDF5 underpins petabytes of science and AI training data. Longevity is real, but financial robustness is thin.

name: Jubilee (Machine Agency, University of Washington)
subcategory: open-source tool-changing motion platform (3D printing, plotting, lab automation)
key_takeaway: Jubilee shows the academic open-hardware route into self-driving labs: a university-designed, OSHWA-certified toolchanger that labs can build for about $1,350, with almost no commercial ecosystem. It is cheap and adaptable but thin on long-term maintenance and supply.

name: Kitware, Inc.
subcategory: open-source scientific visualization, imaging and build tooling; R&D services
latest_value_type: annual consolidated revenue, stated as 'more than $39 million' (year not given on the page)
key_takeaway: Kitware is the best US example of a services company sustaining open scientific infrastructure for decades without VC, an exit or relicensing: government R&D contracts paid to build open tools, and the tools' ubiquity sells more contracts. The model is durable but caps growth at services scale.

name: LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator), Sandia National Laboratories
subcategory: classical molecular dynamics code
key_takeaway: LAMMPS shows a national-lab code outliving the industrial CRADA that created it by opening up: 30 years on it is a GPL community platform and a default MD engine for ML potentials, with no revenue model. Its fragility is people, not licence: a small DOE-funded core team carries maintenance for a very large user base.

name: The Linux Foundation
subcategory: 'foundation of foundations' hosting open-source projects (501(c)(6) trade association)
latest_value_type: annual revenue, IRS Form 990, fiscal year ending Dec 2024 (expenses $204,369,300; net assets $144.6M)
key_takeaway: With $221M revenue (2024), the Linux Foundation dwarfs the science-relevant open foundations in this group (NumFOCUS $8.4M in 2024; the ASF $2.2M in FY2025; the RCSB PDB's federal award is about $49M over five years). In 2024-2026 it absorbed AI-era projects (PyTorch, Jupyter, MCP), so corporate-funded foundations, not science agencies, increasingly govern the open tools that AI-for-science depends on.

name: The Materials Project (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
subcategory: computed materials-property database (DFT) and open-source tools
key_takeaway: The Materials Project is the clearest physical-science case of government-funded open data becoming AI training infrastructure: a DOE lab project with no revenue model now underpins commercial materials-AI efforts at Google DeepMind and Microsoft. Its value is enormous in usage terms but invisible financially (no published budget), and its main risks are federal-funding dependence and creeping licence fragmentation when industry contributes data on its own terms.

name: NumFOCUS, Inc.
subcategory: fiscal sponsor for open-source scientific computing projects
latest_value_type: annual revenue, IRS Form 990, fiscal year ending Dec 2024 (expenses $11,090,430)
key_takeaway: NumFOCUS is the main US nonprofit sustaining the scientific Python stack, at about $8-11M a year, small relative to the commercial AI value built on NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn. Its 2023-2024 deficits and Jupyter's move to the Linux Foundation suggest that community fiscal sponsors are being outcompeted by better-funded corporate-backed foundations.

name: OpenFlexure Microscope (OpenFlexure Project)
subcategory: open-source 3D-printed motorised optical microscope
key_takeaway: OpenFlexure is the clearest open-hardware example in this group: grant-funded academic design, commercialised by independent small vendors rather than a spin-out, with reach (50+ countries) far beyond what the university team could manufacture. Its limit is that open designs do not carry medical certification, which still needs a liable manufacturer.

name: OpenFOAM (OpenFOAM Foundation / CFD Direct; OpenCFD Ltd under ESI Group and Keysight)
subcategory: computational fluid dynamics (CFD) toolkit
key_takeaway: OpenFOAM is the open CFD comparator to Ansys: comparable reach, but its maintainers run on about EUR 250k a year while Ansys sold for $35B. GPL licensing protected the code through three changes of corporate owner and a developer split, but did not solve sustainability; the Foundation's own 2025 appeal says funding must double.

name: Project Jupyter
subcategory: interactive computing (notebooks, JupyterLab, JupyterHub, kernels)
latest_value_type: joint philanthropic grant (Helmsley Trust, Moore Foundation, Sloan Foundation), 2015; no current annual budget found
key_takeaway: Jupyter is the archetype of academic open-science software becoming industry infrastructure for the AI era: a physics student's tool became the front end of Google Colab and SageMaker. Its sustainability path ran from philanthropy (Sloan, Moore, Helmsley) to a corporate-funded Linux Foundation entity, showing how value captured by big platforms is partly routed back through foundations.

name: PyLabRobot
subcategory: hardware-agnostic Python SDK for lab automation (liquid handlers, plate readers, etc.)
key_takeaway: PyLabRobot is the young (2022), academic-origin open layer for lab automation, analogous to what Linux drivers did for hardware: it opens closed instruments to programmatic and AI control. Its reach is growing quickly, but it has no visible funding model beyond contributor time and vendor support.

name: Quantum ESPRESSO (Quantum ESPRESSO Foundation)
subcategory: plane-wave density-functional theory (DFT) suite
key_takeaway: Quantum ESPRESSO is the open, foundation-governed counterpart to VASP: comparable scientific reach (tens of thousands of citations) funded by European public research money and a non-profit that holds the copyright. It is a non-US comparator showing that the open model in DFT depends on public HPC programmes such as MaX/EuroHPC rather than on licence sales.

name: RCSB Protein Data Bank and the Worldwide Protein Data Bank (wwPDB)
subcategory: macromolecular structure archive (experimental 3D structures)
latest_value_type: multi-year federal award for RCSB PDB core operations, 2024 to 2028 (not annual; prior 2019-2023 period was $34.3M). RCSB separately estimates archive replacement cost at >$27B.
key_takeaway: The PDB is the strongest evidence that long-lived, government-founded open scientific data pays off on timescales no market would fund: a 1971 national-lab archive costing roughly $10M a year in US federal support became the substrate for a Nobel-winning AI system 50 years later. Its robustness comes from international replication and a public-domain licence, not from any single institution.

name: RDKit
subcategory: open-source cheminformatics and molecular machine-learning toolkit
key_takeaway: RDKit is the open-source chemistry analogue of the scientific Python stack: free, permissive, and woven into nearly every molecular-ML workflow, with usage (millions of downloads per month) far outrunning its visible funding. It is a prime example of AI-era value accruing on top of thinly resourced open infrastructure.

name: VASP Software GmbH (Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package)
subcategory: plane-wave density-functional theory (DFT) code
key_takeaway: VASP is the clearest closed counterpoint in physical-science software: an academic code that commercialised through group licences, kept source confidential, and in 2026 explicitly barred AI training on its code. It shows that closed scientific software can be long-lived and high-impact, while open data built on its outputs (Materials Project) ended up becoming the AI training resource.

name: Zenodo (CERN / OpenAIRE)
subcategory: general-purpose open research repository (data, software, papers) with DOIs
key_takeaway: Zenodo shows the 'public lab as host' model: an EU-commissioned, CERN-operated repository that is free to use because it rides on CERN's physics infrastructure and EC grants. Its July 2026 AI notice states that uploaded files are not used to train AI models, a deliberate contrast with how other open archives have become AI training data.

name: 3D Systems Corporation
subcategory: industrial 3D printers (SLA, SLS, MJP, CJP, direct metal printing), materials and healthcare solutions
key_takeaway: 3D Systems is the original closed AM incumbent: founded on Hull's 1986 SLA patent, enforced against newcomers, and enlarged through acquisitions in the 2012-2014 bubble. Its decline since then (a market cap down roughly 97% from the 2013 peak, divestiture of its software in 2025) shows that patents and proprietary ecosystems gave a head start, not durability. For a lab, its sale of the 3DXpert metal-AM software is a reminder that closed tool chains can change hands or disappear.

name: Aconity3D GmbH
subcategory: research-grade, open-parameter laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) machines; also DED (wire) and polymer SLS
key_takeaway: Aconity3D shows a third path between open-source hardware and closed incumbents: proprietary machines sold as open research instruments, with every laser parameter and sensor stream exposed for analysis and publication. For a lab developing LPBF aluminium alloys and aiming for self-driving experiments, that open process access, not open CAD files, is the openness that matters, and it is a criterion to require when buying closed instruments.

name: arXiv
subcategory: preprint server (physics, mathematics, computer science and five other areas); independent nonprofit since 1 July 2026
key_takeaway: arXiv is the long-lived success of open, nonprofit science infrastructure: in 35 years it went from a national-lab physics archive to an independent nonprofit running on a budget under $9M. Its 2025-26 history shows a new risk to openness in the age of AI. Generative tools inflate submission volume faster than moderation can scale, so 'free to submit' now comes with rate limits and quality gates. Its robustness model is diversified support from member libraries, Simons, Schmidt Sciences, NASA, NSF, XTX and Siegel, rather than one patron.

name: Automata Technologies Ltd
subcategory: lab automation platform for life sciences (LINQ Bench modular hardware + LINQ orchestration software)
key_takeaway: Automata is the venture-backed newcomer in lab automation: architects turned robot-arm makers turned life-science bench builders, with at least $135M raised since 2022 and a 2026 AI-lab pitch backed by Danaher. Like Opentrons' 2026 messaging, it redefines 'open' as API access rather than open licences, so labs gain scriptability but not the ability to fork or repair the system.

name: Carbon, Inc.
subcategory: resin 3D printing (CLIP / Digital Light Synthesis), proprietary dual-cure resins and production software
key_takeaway: Carbon is the private, closed, materials-first AM unicorn: a 2013 chemistry startup valued at about $2.5B in 2019 that never went public, raised a small $60M insider round in 2025 and in 2026 still enforces its foundational dual-cure patent. Its CEO's view that materials, not printers, decide the opportunity is the same thesis the Digital Alloy Lab works on, but applied to proprietary resins instead of open alloy data.

name: Center for Open Science (COS) / OSF
subcategory: nonprofit research-transparency organisation; OSF (Open Science Framework) platform, OSF Registries and OSF Preprints
key_takeaway: COS shows the funding ceiling of philanthropy-built open infrastructure. About $69M of contributions and grants (2013-2024, Form 990s), with the Arnold Foundation the largest listed sponsor every year to 2019, built the best-known open-science platform. Yet in 2026 OSF stopped accepting new projects because COS could not raise $4-5M a year to run it. Its response is instructive: keep the unique, low-cost functions (preregistration, preprints, linking), hand storage to CERN-backed Zenodo and others, and fund the continuity of public records. A lab relying on any single free open-science service

name: Desktop Metal, Inc.
subcategory: metal and polymer additive manufacturing (binder jetting, bound metal deposition, photopolymer)
key_takeaway: Desktop Metal is the clearest bust of the 2020-21 AM SPAC wave: an MIT-founded, $438M-venture-funded closed metal-AM company that listed at up to $2.5B in December 2020, lost most of its value, was bought by Nano Dimension for $5.295 a share in April 2025 and filed for Chapter 11 in July 2025. For a lab buying closed metal-AM tools, it shows that a vendor's survival risk becomes the lab's: sintering recipes, software and service disappear with the company unless the lab owns open process data.

name: Digital Science (Holtzbrinck Publishing Group), incl. Figshare
subcategory: commercial research-infrastructure group; Figshare general-purpose data repository (proprietary SaaS hosting openly licensed content), plus Dimensions, Altmetric, Overleaf, ReadCube, Symplectic
key_takeaway: Digital Science shows the commercial route to open-science infrastructure: a publisher-owned group (Holtzbrinck) that backed a PhD student's data-sharing tool in 2012 and turned it into institutional SaaS, while keeping the content openly licensed and the code closed. Researchers get free, DOI-backed open data deposit; institutions and funders get a vendor, not a commons, so portability rests on DOIs and APIs rather than forkable code.

name: EOS GmbH Electro Optical Systems
subcategory: industrial laser powder-bed fusion (DMLS/LPBF) metal and polymer (SLS) systems, materials and software
key_takeaway: EOS is the reference closed LPBF incumbent: a Munich family company that commercialised DMLS in 1996, settled its patent war with 3D Systems by cross-licensing, and sells machines, materials and 'validated' parameters from a single source on subscription. Its durability (about EUR 360M revenue, no outside investors) contrasts with the SPAC-funded US metal-AM entrants. For an LPBF aluminium-alloy lab, EOS sets the closed, validated-parameter benchmark (AlSi10Mg, AlF357, Al5X1, Al2139 AM, Constellium CP1), and its parameter and software model is the opposite of open science.

name: Hamilton Company (Reno, NV) and Hamilton AG (formerly Hamilton Bonaduz AG, Switzerland)
subcategory: automated liquid handling (STAR line), precision syringes, sample storage, process-analytics sensors; sister Hamilton Medical (ventilators) (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Hamilton is the closed, family-owned incumbent of liquid handling: founded in a garage in 1950, never listed or VC-funded, and still privately held with ~3,000 staff. Its STAR robots are proprietary, yet the open PyLabRobot driver lets labs program them in MIT-licensed Python and port protocols to other brands, showing how open software can wrap a closed instrument without the vendor's involvement.

name: Kardex Holding AG
subcategory: automated storage and retrieval: vertical lift modules (Kardex Shuttle), carousels, AutoStore systems, high-bay warehouses (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Kardex represents the closed, mature logistics-automation incumbents that labs end up buying: a 1898 filing-system brand reborn as a Swiss listed company (EUR 850M revenue, ~2,960 staff in 2025) selling proprietary vertical lift modules and AutoStore systems. It is profitable and stable but entirely closed, so labs that automate storage depend on its interfaces and service.

name: Markforged Holding Corporation (MarkForged, Inc.)
subcategory: composite (continuous carbon fibre) FFF and bound-metal 3D printers, 'Digital Forge' platform
key_takeaway: Markforged is a SPAC-era closed-hardware story: about $137M of venture money and a ~$2.1B SPAC valuation in 2021, then a 1-for-10 reverse split, a patent loss, a $116M take-private by Nano Dimension in 2025 and a $42.5M resale to Stratasys in 2026. Its proprietary, cloud-tied printers changed hands twice in thirteen months, which is the vendor-continuity risk a lab takes on when it buys closed AM hardware.

name: OpenCalphad
subcategory: free/open-source CALPHAD thermodynamic software (Fortran) with an application software interface (OCASI)
key_takeaway: OpenCalphad is the 'scientists' open CALPHAD': a GPL-style Fortran code started at a German materials institute in 2013, co-written by Thermo-Calc-generation CALPHAD veterans, and kept alive by an informal international collaboration. It proves an open, independent CALPHAD engine is feasible. Like pycalphad it lacks open assessed databases and AM process models, and it relies on one maintainer's repository, so it complements rather than replaces commercial tools for an LPBF alloy lab.

name: OurResearch (legal name Impactstory; now operating as OpenAlex)
subcategory: nonprofit open scholarly metadata (OpenAlex), open-access discovery (Unpaywall) and library analytics (Unsub)
key_takeaway: OurResearch shows a small nonprofit building core open-science infrastructure on a few million dollars a year (FY2025 revenue $4.3M, 56% of it grants) by selling services around CC0 data. Its finances were fragile, with negative net assets in FY2024, until large grants such as Arcadia's $7.5M arrived, and it now prices heavy API use. For a lab, OpenAlex is the open literature database that this very project uses, and its CC0 snapshot protects users from any later pricing change.

name: Papers with Code (Meta AI)
subcategory: free index linking ML papers to code, leaderboards (SOTA tables), methods and datasets
key_takeaway: Papers with Code is the clearest case of open science infrastructure held by a big tech owner: a 2018 project whose CC BY-SA leaderboards became the standard record of ML progress, whose team moved inside Facebook AI and trained Meta's Galactica science LLM on the literature, and which was left to decay and redirected to Hugging Face in mid-2025. The open data licence let the community archive and revive it; the corporate hosting is what failed.

name: pycalphad (PyCalphad Development Team)
subcategory: open-source CALPHAD computational thermodynamics library in Python
key_takeaway: pycalphad is the open counterpart to Thermo-Calc. Born of a NASA fellowship and MIT-licensed, it does the core CALPHAD equilibrium calculations in Python and reads the incumbent's TDB format. It shows how an open tool can cheaply win scripting and automation use, while the closed vendor keeps the high-value data. Its fragility is people, not licence: two maintainers wrote about three-quarters of the commits, and no sustained funding is visible.

name: Stratasys Ltd.
subcategory: polymer 3D printers (FDM, PolyJet, SAF, P3/Origin, Neo SLA), materials and GrabCAD software
