key_takeaway: Stratasys is the surviving closed polymer-AM incumbent: a 1989 FDM-patent company that grew through mergers, bought MakerBot just after MakerBot closed its designs, fought off or failed in three 2023 consolidation attempts, and in 2026 buys distressed peers (MarkForged for $42.5M) with a debt-free balance sheet. It shows that closed incumbents can outlast SPAC-era entrants, but at a fraction of their 2013 value, and that 'open' in its vocabulary means licensed access to third-party materials.

name: Tecan Group AG
subcategory: laboratory automation and liquid handling (Freedom EVO, Fluent), OEM instrument components and contract manufacturing (closed comparator)
key_takeaway: Tecan is the archetypal closed liquid-handling incumbent: founded by four engineers in 1980, listed since 1999 and built on proprietary Genesis, Freedom EVO and Fluent platforms plus OEM manufacturing. Its 2021 COVID peak and largest-ever acquisition were followed by four years of falling sales and a 77% fall in market value to end-2025. For an open lab, Tecan robots are usable mainly through community open-source drivers that Tecan does not sponsor.

name: Thermo-Calc Software AB
subcategory: closed CALPHAD computational thermodynamics and kinetics (Thermo-Calc, DICTRA, TC-PRISMA, AM Module, databases)
key_takeaway: Thermo-Calc is the closed incumbent that defines the CALPHAD workflow an LPBF alloy lab uses. A KTH research code became a foundation-owned company in 1997, and it sells licences, databases and now services, with a scriptable but proprietary Python API. Its longevity (development since 1977) and steady releases show that a closed academic spin-off can be durable without venture capital. For a lab that wants to work openly, the practical split is to use Thermo-Calc for the commercial databases and the AM module, and to publish assessments as TDB files and workflows in pycalphad, so others can r

name: Universal Robots A/S and Mobile Industrial Robots ApS (Teradyne Robotics)
subcategory: collaborative robot arms (cobots) and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs); Teradyne's Robotics segment
key_takeaway: Universal Robots shows the 'open interface, closed machine' model at scale: a university spin-out that sold a closed cobot, published open-source drivers so labs and integrators could program it from ROS, sold itself to Teradyne for $285M in 2015 and reached 100,000 units. A decade later the combined UR and MiR segment is shrinking and loss-making ($308M revenue, $99M pre-tax loss and ~400 job cuts in 2025), a reminder that a lab's open control code is portable while the closed arm it drives depends on one vendor's fortunes.

name: Velo3D, Inc.
subcategory: laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) metal printers and contract production (Sapphire)
key_takeaway: Velo3D is the third 2021 metal-AM SPAC and the one that survived by being recapitalised rather than sold: after its value fell more than 90%, a creditor took 95% of the equity in 2024, and it relisted on Nasdaq in 2025 as a defense-focused producer with a going-concern warning. For an LPBF alloy lab it is the archetype of the closed, recipe-locked production printer, good at qualified parts and poor as an open research instrument.

name: AlphaFold 2 and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database
subcategory: protein structure prediction model and open structure database
key_takeaway: The reference case for open AI-for-science: a corporate lab released permissive code, weights (after a six-month non-commercial phase) and a public-institution-hosted database built from public PDB data. It produced field-wide adoption and a Nobel Prize. The same lab then restricted its successor (AlphaFold 3).

name: AlphaFold 3
subcategory: biomolecular complex structure prediction (proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, modifications)
forks: Open AF3-class models: Boltz-1/2 (MIT), Chai-1 (Apache-2.0 from 2024-11-27), OpenFold3 (Apache-2.0 per GitHub; MIT per Wikipedia), Protenix (Apache 2.0, per Wikipedia)
key_takeaway: AlphaFold 3 is the clearest closing event in AI for science. A corporate owner with a commercial route (Isomorphic Labs) withheld code and weights, and the community answered with permissive clones. Over two years Google re-opened the code in stages but never the weights. Labs relying on AF3 should prefer an MIT/Apache clone wherever commercial use or redistribution matters.

name: Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 (Boltz PBC)
subcategory: open AF3-class biomolecular structure and binding-affinity models
key_takeaway: Boltz shows the lifecycle of an open clone: an academic MIT release fills the gap left by a restricted corporate model, wins users, becomes a company and then closes its newest models. Labs should pin MIT versions and keep the training data, which remain usable whatever the company does.

name: Chai-1 (Chai Discovery)
subcategory: AF3-class biomolecular structure prediction
key_takeaway: A startup used an open (eventually Apache-2.0) model as a calling card while keeping its frontier model closed, a typical AI-startup open-core pattern.

name: CHGNet (Crystal Hamiltonian Graph Neural Network)
subcategory: charge-informed universal interatomic potential
key_takeaway: A DOE-lab academic model, fully open in code, weights and data. Publishing the training set multiplied its impact beyond the model itself.

name: ESM protein language models (Meta FAIR, then EvolutionaryScale, now Biohub)
subcategory: protein language models, structure prediction and generative protein design
key_takeaway: Openness tracked the owner's incentives: open at Meta, restricted at a VC-backed startup, open again under a philanthropic non-profit. Download counts show how much more the permissive models were used.

name: Evo 2 (Arc Institute)
subcategory: genomic (DNA) foundation model across all domains of life
key_takeaway: The fullest release in the group: a non-profit published a 40B frontier-scale model with its training data under Apache-2.0. Non-profit, philanthropically funded labs are the most reliable source of fully open AI for science.

name: GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration)
subcategory: crystal stability prediction and materials discovery
key_takeaway: GNoME is the materials-science counterpart of AlphaFold 3's restriction: corporate model, public training data (Materials Project), non-commercial outputs, no weights. It also imported a non-commercial carve-out into a public database.

name: M3GNet and MatGL (Materials Graph Library)
subcategory: universal graph interatomic potential and property models
key_takeaway: Open academic architectures become the substrate for corporate models. Durability depends on continued maintenance more than on the licence.

name: MACE foundation models (MACE-MP-0 and successors)
subcategory: universal machine-learned interatomic potentials
key_takeaway: Academic does not always mean permissive. The same group publishes MIT and non-commercial models. Licence choice for models trained on CC BY data is unconstrained, so it reflects the developer's commercialisation strategy.

name: Matbench and Matbench Discovery (materials ML benchmarks)
subcategory: open benchmarks and leaderboards for materials property prediction and ML interatomic potentials
key_takeaway: Benchmarks are a cheap, high-leverage public good: small MIT repos at a DOE project anchor how the whole field reports progress.

name: MatterGen (Microsoft Research)
subcategory: generative model for inorganic crystal design
key_takeaway: A corporate lab can release a physical-science model fully open (MIT code and weights, open training data) when the business (Azure) does not depend on the model. Compare the same lab's MatterSim, whose best versions are reserved for Azure.

name: MatterSim (Microsoft Research)
subcategory: universal machine-learned interatomic potential
key_takeaway: Within one corporate lab, the model that sits next to a cloud product (MatterSim) is open core, while the one that does not (MatterGen) is fully open.

name: Meta FAIR Chemistry: Open Catalyst, OMat24, OMol25 and UMA
subcategory: open DFT datasets and universal interatomic potentials (catalysis, materials, molecules, MOFs)
key_takeaway: Meta is the most generous corporate data publisher in materials and chemistry (hundreds of millions of DFT calculations, CC BY 4.0). It uses Llama-style custom licences for the models. Data openness, not weight openness, has had the larger spillover.

name: NVIDIA BioNeMo Framework and ALCHEMI Toolkit-Ops
subcategory: GPU frameworks, recipes and accelerated checkpoints for biology (BioNeMo) and atomistic chemistry (ALCHEMI)
key_takeaway: The hardware vendor's open science is complementary-goods strategy: Apache-2.0 frameworks and accelerated versions of other people's open models, with value captured in GPUs and enterprise services.

name: OpenFold and OpenFold3
subcategory: open, trainable reproductions of AlphaFold 2 and AlphaFold 3
key_takeaway: Academic and consortium reproductions are how restricted corporate models become open science. OpenFold shows that the training data (MSAs) and the training code, not only the weights, are the scarce public goods.

name: Orb models (Orbital Materials)
subcategory: universal interatomic potentials (materials and molecules)
key_takeaway: Startups in materials AI tend to open the model and close the application, the reverse of the protein startups (Chai, Boltz) that open older models and close the newest.

name: RoseTTAFold and RFdiffusion family (Baker lab)
subcategory: protein structure prediction and generative protein design
key_takeaway: An academic lab chose permissive weight licences for its generative design models, the opposite trajectory to the corporate lab. That made RFdiffusion and the MPNN models the open default for protein design.

name: SevenNet (Scalable EquiVariance-Enabled Neural Network)
subcategory: universal interatomic potentials with parallel MD
key_takeaway: Academic MLIP licences are converging on permissive terms, but not uniformly. Check the licence of each checkpoint, not only the code.
